entries.name: Techno-X USA Inc. v. Spartan Forge LLC et al.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Consent defense to the Exclusivity breach: rejected. Angers permitted only one information-gathering call and never consented to transaction discussions (Thompson concession).
"Never fully negotiated" defense: rejected. The governing text reaches the "decision to... negotiate," not only a completed deal.

Waiver and acquiescence: rejected. Both are affirmative defenses on which Spartan Forge bore the burden, and both require full knowledge, which Techno-X lacked because the PRADCO talks were concealed.
Ratification: rejected. It requires knowledge, and Techno-X's Dec. 18 objection and suit defeat it.
Managing Member authority under § 8.1(a): rejected, because that grant is expressly "Subject to Section 8.2."
"Advisory" Board characterization: rejected under §§ 8.4 and 8.2, since otherwise those provisions would be surplusage.
Standing defense to the claims relating to Angers as director: abandoned by Spartan Forge post-trial (Emerald Partners).
Information-rights claims beyond § 7.2(c): waived by Techno-X (fn. 197).

Techno-X's § 8.2(b)(iv) and (b)(i) claims: rejected. An asset sale is not a merger or consolidation, and the separately defined "Sale of the Company" (§ 1, § 9.5(e)) shows deliberate drafting. No material change in "Company Business" was proven.
Techno-X's § 8.4 claim: rejected as redundant of § 8.2, with no independent breach.
Techno-X's § 9.9 claim: rejected, because the provision imposes no duty to circulate advance materials.

Counterclaim ground § 9.6(b)(ix)(c): rejected. The incomplete agenda was not a material breach. Even assuming materiality, any default was cured because a meeting was scheduled within the 10-day cure period. The prevention doctrine also bars Spartan Forge from exploiting nonperformance it caused.

Counterclaim ground § 9.6(b)(ix)(e): rejected for insufficient evidence of "material harm" under its Black's dictionary meaning. The marketing and integration theory fails because § 9.8 contemplated a services agreement first, Angers reasonably treated a finalized services agreement as a prerequisite, and the agreement failed because Spartan Forge delayed it to pursue PRADCO.

After-acquired evidence (applied arguendo, "even if the doctrine applies in this context"): rejected. The "kill" documents (JX 348/85/139/407) reflect contingency planning, not breach or material harm, and the post hoc justification was "contrived" bad-faith re-justification.
Prior material breach and unclean hands defenses against Techno-X: rejected (n.249), because Techno-X came into equity with clean hands. These rulings do not resolve the phase-two counterclaims.
Techno-X's own prior-breach and good-faith defenses to the counterclaim: not reached (fn. 214).

Laches as a bar to setting aside the redemption: rejected (n.259). The notice's validity was already being litigated when the redemption occurred, Techno-X rejected the consideration and promptly moved to preserve the status quo (Dkt. 131), and any prejudice was self-inflicted.
Rescission or quasi-appraisal (damages-only) framing: rejected. Damages are inadequate for the loss of unique governance rights, and Techno-X does not seek rescission.
Techno-X's request to extend exclusivity: denied. The period expired in March 2025, PRADCO withdrew on suit, there is no proof of later negotiations, and a new period would expand the bargain.

Techno-X's request for a permanent injunction: denied. A PRADCO ban is overbroad because §§ 8.2(a)(v) and (xi) require Board and Majority in Interest approval, not Techno-X's individual consent, so a ban would create a blocking right a 6% holder with one of three directors lacks. A narrower compliance injunction is unnecessary given declaratory relief and would enjoin hypothetical breaches.
Techno-X's request for bad-faith fee shifting: denied. Discovery misconduct was already sanctioned (Dkt. 54), and aggressive but unsuccessful positions are not clear evidence of subjective bad faith.

authorities_cited.proposition: Declaratory Judgment Act basis for Spartan Forge's counterclaim and for the declaration that the Nov. 20, 2024 notice and the Apr. 30, 2025 redemption are invalid.

authorities_cited.authority: Term Sheet Exclusivity Provision; LLC Agreement §§ 1, 7.2(c), 8.1(a), 8.2(a)(v), 8.2(a)(xi), 8.2(b)(i), 8.2(b)(iv), 8.4, 9.5(e), 9.6(b)(ix)(c), 9.6(b)(ix)(e), 9.8, 9.9, 11.10
authorities_cited.proposition: Operative consent, governance, information, Withdrawal Event/Involuntary Termination, purchase-right and Alignment Meeting provisions. Fn. 160 notes the agreement contains two § 8.2(a)(v)s and holds the second applies.
Preponderance of the evidence burden.
Elements of breach of contract.

authorities_cited.authority: Salamone, 106 A.3d at 367-68; Osborn, 991 A.2d at 1159-60; GMG Cap., 36 A.3d at 779; Rhone-Poulenc, 616 A.2d at 1195; Kuhn Constr., 990 A.2d at 396-97
authorities_cited.proposition: Contract interpretation: objective theory, four corners, plain meaning, no surplusage.
Use of distinct defined terms reflects deliberate drafting, so an asset sale is not a merger or consolidation under § 8.2(b).
Waiver and acquiescence are affirmative defenses on which the defendant bears the burden.

authorities_cited.authority: Klaassen, 106 A.3d at 1047-48; Coinmint, 261 A.3d at 893
authorities_cited.proposition: Waiver and acquiescence require full knowledge.

authorities_cited.authority: TR Invs. v. Genger, 2010 WL 2901704, at *15 (citing Frank v. Wilson, 32 A.2d at 283)
authorities_cited.proposition: Ratification requires knowledge.
Prompt objection and suit defeat ratification.
Arguments not pursued post-trial are abandoned (here, the standing defense).
Nominal damages are awarded for a technical breach without cognizable harm.

authorities_cited.authority: 2009 Caiola, 2015 WL 6007596, at *18; BioLife, 838 A.2d at 278; Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 241
authorities_cited.proposition: Materiality standard for breach; the incomplete agenda was not material.
Cure within the contractual period defeats a default-based termination.

authorities_cited.authority: W & G Seaford, 714 F. Supp. 1336, 1341 (citing Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 245); De Los Santos, 2025 WL 2092402, at *5 n.54
authorities_cited.proposition: Prevention doctrine: a party cannot exploit nonperformance it caused (n.224).

authorities_cited.authority: Lorillard, 903 A.2d at 738; ShiftKey, 2025 WL 548420, at *12; Black's Law Dictionary (12th ed.)
authorities_cited.proposition: Dictionaries supply the plain meaning of undefined terms such as "material harm" (n.229).
Under the after-acquired evidence doctrine, the justification must be learned after termination and must independently support it (applied arguendo).

authorities_cited.authority: Costanzo, 339 A.3d at 1261 n.153 (citing Harbor Ins., 922 F.2d at 363)
authorities_cited.proposition: Trying on a new defense after a pretextual one fails is bad faith.
Plans to compete are not a breach where performance continued.
A sabotage theory fails where no action was taken on the plans.
A party may not rely on retroactively invented grounds for termination.
A for-cause predicate cannot be circumvented.
Unclean hands standard; Techno-X came into equity with clean hands (n.249).
Cited cf. for reinstating a member's interest and attendant rights after an invalid removal.
Cited cf. for the point that damages are inadequate for the loss of unique governance rights.
Laches test (n.259).

authorities_cited.authority: Krafton, 354 A.3d at 952-53; Tri State Mall, 298 A.2d at 371-72
authorities_cited.proposition: Equitable extension of contractual deadlines lost to the counterparty's wrongful conduct.
A party cannot rely on the failure of a condition its own breach materially caused.
Cited cf. for the point that equitable relief cannot expand the parties' bargain; supports denying a new exclusivity period.
Courts do not enjoin hypothetical future breaches.
American Rule on attorneys' fees.

authorities_cited.authority: Gatz, 59 A.3d at 1222; Auriga, 40 A.3d at 880; Shawe v. Elting, 157 A.3d at 150
authorities_cited.proposition: The bad-faith fee-shifting exception is not invoked lightly and requires clear evidence of subjective bad faith.
Aggressive but unsuccessful litigation positions are not bad faith.

summary.brief_summary: In phase one of a bifurcated post-trial proceeding, minority investor Techno-X USA Inc. (Vosker Corporation's Delaware subsidiary) sued Spartan Forge LLC and its Managing Member Thompson over a concealed $20M PRADCO asset sale, and Spartan Forge counterclaimed for a declaration validating its Involuntary Termination and redemption of Techno-X. The Court found the secret negotiations breached the Term Sheet Exclusivity Provision and the § 8.2(a) approval requirements, and rejected the consent, waiver, acquiescence, ratification and managerial-authority defenses for lack of knowledge or under the contract's text. It held the termination pretextual: the Alignment Meeting default was immaterial, cured and caused by defendants themselves, no material harm was proven, and the after-acquired justifications were contrived. It reinstated Techno-X and extended its contractual deadlines, but declined to extend exclusivity, enjoin the Company or shift fees.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether Spartan Forge LLC (the "Company") and its Managing Member, William J. Thompson, breached the Term Sheet Exclusivity Provision and the LLC Agreement's consent, governance and information provisions by secretly negotiating a $20M asset sale to PRADCO/Moultrie without the consent of Techno-X USA Inc. (the "Investor") or Board/Majority in Interest approval. A second question was whether the Company's Involuntary Termination of Techno-X, noticed Nov. 20, 2024 under LLC Agreement § 9.6(b)(ix)(c) (uncured Alignment Meeting default) and (e) (material harm to financial prospects), and the Apr. 30, 2025 redemption that followed were valid. If not, the Court had to decide what equitable relief (reinstatement, deadline extensions, exclusivity extension, injunction, fees) was warranted.
summary.holding: Judgment for Techno-X on (i) the Term Sheet Exclusivity Provision and LLC Agreement §§ 8.2(a)(v) and (xi) against Spartan Forge, (ii) § 7.2(c) against Thompson as Managing Member ($1.00 nominal damages for a technical breach without cognizable harm), and (iii) Spartan Forge's declaratory counterclaim. Judgment for defendants on Techno-X's §§ 8.2(b), 8.4 and 9.9 claims. Neither Involuntary Termination ground was established, so no Withdrawal Event occurred. The (c) ground failed because the Alignment Meeting default was immaterial, was in any event cured, and was barred by the prevention doctrine. The (e) ground failed for lack of proof of material harm, and the after-acquired evidence justification (assumed arguendo) was contingency planning and a contrived pretext. Under 10 Del. C. § 6501, the Nov. 20, 2024 notice and the Apr. 30, 2025 redemption are declared invalid and set aside. Techno-X retains its 6% Series A Preferred Units and its governance, consent and information rights, but the expired Exclusivity Provision is not revived (n.254). Equitable extensions: (a) the § 9.9 24-month Alignment Meeting period is extended by 694 days; (b) the § 9.8 services agreement deadline is reset to 60 days after the implementing order; (c) the Majority Right to Purchase (12-month) and External Valuation (24-month) periods are each extended by 694 days, still conditioned on execution of the services agreement, with all other § 9.8 timing unchanged. Denied: a new exclusivity period, a permanent injunction (PRADCO ban or compliance injunction), and fee shifting; each side bears its own fees and costs. The implementing order must cancel the unaccepted check and note, conform membership records, recognize Angers as Board designee and provide information rights. A proposed implementing order is due within 10 business days, and the parties must confer and file a proposed scheduling order for the phase-two claims.
key_facts_and_concessions: The Term Sheet (Mar. 8, 2024) contains a 12-month Exclusivity Provision. Absent Techno-X consent, it bars soliciting, participating in or responding to discussions on financing, securities or material-asset sales, and bars providing services to Vosker competitors. The June 9 Summary Judgment Letter Opinion held that its binding provisions survive the LLC Agreement integration clause (§ 11.10) and that the Feb. 11 amendment resolutions were ineffective.

LLC Agreement (May 17, 2024) terms: Techno-X holds 6% Series A Preferred Units, stepping up to 12% through $500K plus 15 payments of $70,666.66. Under § 9.8, the Majority Right to Purchase (60% at a $15.6M valuation within 12 months of first issuance) and the Global purchase right (15% discount, 120 days) are both conditioned on a services agreement within 60 days, a deadline extended to Oct. 31, 2024. § 9.9 requires quarterly Alignment Meetings.

Thompson secretly negotiated the PRADCO/Moultrie asset sale, progressing from term sheets in August to an LOI on Oct. 29 and a draft APA on Dec. 3. He signed the LOI the same day he refused to sign the services agreement, even though all services-agreement issues had been resolved by Oct. 29.

Angers authorized only a single information-gathering call ("don't say to[o] much"). Thompson conceded Angers never consented to transaction discussions (Tr. 629-31) and that the PRADCO deal overlapped the Vosker integration (Tr. 659).

Belser's Oct. 16 "Declaration of Independence" email (JX 555) planned to "delay everything," manufacture an uncured Alignment Meeting default, shed Vosker and sell. Belser and Thompson plotted to catch Techno-X in a breach.

Defendants stalled Laaboudi's meeting requests from Sept. 3 to Oct. 16, then demanded he schedule a meeting "to avoid breaching" (n.225). The Nov. 7 meeting was held without advance materials (Belser Tr. 567-68). Techno-X proposed four continuation dates within the cure period, and none received a response.

Techno-X first learned of the Nov. 20 termination notice at the Dec. 17 Board meeting, which had no agenda (Belser Tr. 572). It objected and sued Dec. 18, and PRADCO withdrew Dec. 19. Techno-X never accepted the redemption check and promissory note.

Vosker kept Spartan Forge afloat by accelerating payments and prepaying for services never performed (n.230). Defendants' material-harm proof consisted solely of Belser's testimony (plus Thompson Tr. 597).
Thompson delivered the 2025 budget, due Oct. 1, 2024 under § 7.2(c), in April 2025, eight minutes before a Board meeting.
Spartan Forge does not challenge the validity or enforceability of the Term Sheet or the LLC Agreement (PTO ¶¶ 48, 52).

The breach of contract, fiduciary duty and tortious interference counterclaims are deferred to phase two (PTO ¶ 27; n.249). The TRO was denied on PRADCO's representation, and the claim against PRADCO was dismissed.
summary.practical_takeaway: A for-cause termination or redemption built on a default the terminating party engineered is vulnerable to the prevention doctrine and to re-equitable deadline extensions measured from the invalid notice. Re-justifying it with after-acquired evidence of contingency planning is likely to be treated as contrived bad faith. Investors seeking post-trial relief should tie each requested injunction or extension to rights they actually hold, since the Court will not create blocking rights or new exclusivity periods beyond the bargain.
summary.standard_of_review: Post-trial (phase one of a bifurcated case). The parties' claims and defenses were decided on a preponderance of the evidence (Revolution Retail), with the burden on Spartan Forge for its affirmative defenses of waiver and acquiescence (Medek). Contracts were construed under Delaware's objective, plain-meaning rules; although the Term Sheet is Quebec-governed, the parties stipulated to Delaware law (fns. 127, 141).

entries.name: Shareholder Representative Services, LLC v. Alexion Pharmaceuticals Inc.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: SRS's request to dismiss the Milestone 1 CRE claim as moot: rejected. The IV-formulation theory failed on the merits, and SRS waived any claim that the 2020 suspension or 2021 termination affected Milestone 1 by limiting its briefing to Milestones 2 through 8, so judgment is entered for Alexion.
SRS's characterization that the Court "did not adjudicate SRS's Milestone 1 CRE claim": rejected (fn. 7). SRS never presented that claim, having identified no Milestone 1 harm from the CRE breach.

SRS's milestone-specific postjudgment interest calculation (rates fixed at historical or predicted milestone due dates): rejected. Postjudgment interest accrues only after judgment and is calculated as of the judgment date.

SRS's request for the floating legal rate on Milestones 4 through 8: rejected. The parties' lawful contract rate governs postjudgment interest, and the Court's prior expectation-damages ruling supports applying the contract rate even to milestones that do not meet the contractual terms, to avoid a windfall.
The damages opinion's earlier general observation favoring a floating legal rate compounded quarterly is effectively superseded. The Court describes the interest issue as addressed iteratively.

authorities_cited.proposition: Alexion covenanted, for seven years after Closing, to use and cause its affiliates (including Syntimmune) to use Commercially Reasonable Efforts to achieve each Milestone Event; this is the basis of Count I.

authorities_cited.authority: S'holder Rep. Serv's LLC v. Alexion Pharms., Inc., 2024 WL 4052343 (Del. Ch. Sept. 5, 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Liability opinion: Milestone 1 was achieved and Alexion breached its payment obligation; the IV-formulation pivot theory failed to show a CRE breach; SRS had to prove harm to prove a CRE breach and identified harm only as to Milestones 2-8.
Issues not briefed are deemed waived; applied to hold SRS waived any claim that the suspension or termination affected Milestone 1.

authorities_cited.authority: S'holder Rep. Serv's LLC v. Alexion Pharms., Inc., 341 A.3d 513, 551 (Del. Ch. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Damages opinion's general observation that quarterly compounding at a floating legal rate was appropriate for postjudgment interest.

authorities_cited.authority: S'holder Rep. Serv's LLC v. Alexion Pharms., Inc., 2025 WL 2993473 (Del. Ch. Oct. 23, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: The contract rate governs prejudgment interest on Milestone 1; expectation-damages principles support applying the contract rate to Milestones 2 and 3 to avoid a windfall; the remaining milestones accrue no prejudgment interest.

authorities_cited.authority: Noranda Aluminum Hldg. Corp. v. XL Ins. Am., Inc., 269 A.3d 974, 979 (Del. 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: Postjudgment interest is owed only after the date of judgment and is calculated as of that date.

authorities_cited.authority: 6 Del. C. § 2031(a) (as cited in fn. 12; fn. 13 cites 6 Del. C. § 2301)
authorities_cited.proposition: The statute applied in Noranda governing the calculation of postjudgment interest.

authorities_cited.authority: Sequoia Presidential Yacht Grp. LLC v. FE P'rs, LLC, 2014 WL 2610577 (Del. Ch. June 12, 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: Delaware uses the parties' specified lawful contract rate to set the postjudgment interest rate (cited "see generally").
The legal-rate statute applied in Sequoia; a lawful contract rate governs postjudgment interest.

authorities_cited.authority: Fortis Advisors LLC v. Johnson & Johnson, 2024 WL 4048060, at *54-55 (Del. Ch. Sept. 4, 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited through the Court's October 2025 ruling for applying the contract rate to milestones not meeting contractual terms to avoid a windfall.
Authority for the Vice Chancellor sitting by designation (see D.I. 467).

summary.brief_summary: After liability and damages opinions in SRS's earn-out suit against Alexion over ALXN1830, the parties disputed two terms of the final order and judgment, which Vice Chancellor Zurn, sitting by designation, resolved by letter. The Court entered judgment for Alexion on the Milestone 1 CRE claim rather than dismissing it as moot: SRS's one theory that reached all milestones failed on the merits, and its post-trial briefing confined CRE harm from its other two theories to Milestones 2-8, so it waived any Milestone 1 harm. On postjudgment interest, the Court rejected SRS's milestone-specific, due-date-anchored calculation and applied the contract rate as of the judgment date to all damages and prejudgment interest, relying on Noranda, the governing contract rate, and its prior expectation-damages ruling.
summary.core_legal_issue: In fixing the terms of the final order and judgment after liability and damages rulings on SRS's earn-out claims: (1) whether Count I's claim that Alexion breached its commercially reasonable efforts ("CRE") covenant (Merger Agreement § 3.8(f)) as to Milestone 1 should be resolved by judgment for Alexion or dismissed as moot, where SRS tied all CRE harm to Milestones 2 through 8; and (2) whether postjudgment interest runs at the contract rate on the full judgment as of the judgment date, or on SRS's milestone-specific basis (Milestone 1 rate fixed at its due date, Milestones 2-3 at record-predicted due dates, Milestones 4-8 at the floating legal rate).
summary.holding: (1) Judgment on Count I as to Milestone 1 will be entered in Alexion's favor, not dismissed as moot. The IV-formulation theory failed to show any CRE breach, and SRS waived any Milestone 1 harm from the 2020 suspension and 2021 termination theories by tying CRE damages exclusively to Milestones 2 through 8. (2) Postjudgment interest runs at the Merger Agreement's contract rate, calculated as of the judgment date, on each damages amount (all milestones) and on prejudgment interest, because postjudgment interest accrues only after judgment, a lawful contract rate governs, and expectation-damages principles support the contract rate even for milestones not meeting contractual terms. The Court expects this to resolve the bond dispute for a stay pending appeal. The parties must alert chambers when ready to file a stipulated final order and judgment with numbers filled in, so it can be entered the same day.
key_facts_and_concessions: The liability opinion found Alexion's fall 2021 HV-108 study satisfied Milestone 1 and that Alexion breached its obligation to pay, then addressed only whether Alexion failed to use CRE to achieve Milestones 2 through 8.

SRS advanced three CRE theories. The theory based on Alexion's pivot away from the IV formulation for the WAIHA indication failed outright to show a CRE breach, which the Court held dooms any Milestone 1 CRE claim on that theory.

For the other two theories (the 2020 suspension of ALXN1830 clinical development and the December 2021 termination of the program after Milestone 1 was reached), SRS's post-trial briefing expressly limited consequences and damages to Milestones 2 through 8 (D.I. 364 at 70, 72, 77, 80). Its reply (D.I. 370) addressed Milestone 1 only as to whether it was achieved (fn. 6).

Per fn. 7, SRS had to prove harm to prove a CRE breach, and the only harm it identified was the failure to achieve Milestones 2 through 8. SRS therefore never presented a Milestone 1 CRE claim for adjudication; it is not that the Court simply failed to adjudicate one.
Count I as pleaded sought at least $370 million, the total of unpaid Earn-Out Payments for Milestone Events (i) through (iii) (fn. 2).

Procedural history on interest: the damages opinion generally observed that quarterly compounding at a floating legal rate (the "modern approach") was appropriate for postjudgment interest. A later ruling, on the contract rate first raised in supplemental briefing, applied the contract rate to prejudgment interest on Milestone 1 and, on expectation-damages principles, on Milestones 2 and 3 (due before the expected judgment date), and awarded no prejudgment interest on the remaining milestones.
Alexion sought the contract rate on the entire judgment as of the judgment date. SRS sought a milestone-specific postjudgment calculation.
The parties dispute the amount of the bond securing a stay pending appeal, which the Court expects this ruling to resolve.
Vice Chancellor Zurn is sitting by designation under Del. Const. art. IV, § 13(2) (fn. 15).
summary.practical_takeaway: A plaintiff that briefs CRE damages only as to later milestones risks an adverse judgment, not a mootness dismissal, on the unbriefed milestone, so post-trial briefs should expressly tie each breach theory to every milestone it is meant to reach. Parties seeking a different postjudgment rate should expect a contractual rate to govern as of the judgment date regardless of when individual payments were or would have been due.
summary.standard_of_review: Not stated. The letter decision resolves disputed terms of the final order and judgment, applying the rule that issues not briefed are waived to the Milestone 1 CRE claim.
